rationale:
Evidence: the best raced design (iterations 6, 8 and 9, score 138.64) has five sensors at y=0.08 spanning x=-0.05 to +0.05 m, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], base_speed 1.0, ki 0.5 and kd 0.6 to 0.8. Across 60 trials it finished 1 of 20 oval runs. Every run still leaves the line at max error about 0.062 m, just past the fixed 0.06 m off-track limit. The body-width term cannot raise that limit, since 0.0125 + body_width/4 stays below 0.06 for any allowed width. Changes that did not move the result: kp 4.0 to 4.5, kd 0.6 to 0.8 (identical metrics), footprint 16 mm to 12 mm (identical score), and speed 0.9 to 1.6 (small effect). Widening the span to +/-0.07 m made things worse. The gains and sensing have plateaued, so the remaining untested lever is steering authority and yaw response.

Changes: (1) wheel_track reduced from 0.12 to 0.09 m. Turn rate is the wheel speed difference divided by wheel_track, so for the same PWM differential the robot yaws about 33 percent faster. This gives more correction authority at the bends where the line is lost. (2) mass reduced from 0.8 to 0.55 kg. Yaw inertia scales with mass, so the robot responds faster to the same turn command and should overshoot less. (3) Controller kept at the best-known settings (base_speed 1.0, ki 0.5, kd 0.8) with kp raised to 5.0 to match the stronger effective steering per PWM count. Sensors and weights are unchanged so only the physical response changes.

Expected result: fewer line-loss events on the s-bend and max error below 0.06 m on at least some oval and s-bend runs, which would raise the finish rate above the current 5 percent. Completion on the slalom remains unlikely. If progress does not move, the next race should test a lower base_speed or search_right line-loss handling.
